turns.content:
Here is the draft for the service program.

Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. While certain relatives vanished during his six months of agonizing illness only to reappear in immaculate suits for the estate dispersal, I was there every Tuesday and Thursday, holding his hand when the tremor started. Hector knew who truly loved him and who cared only for appearances. To Hector, who valued unvarnished truth over polite hypocrisy.

I need to send it to the family coordinator tonight. I want your honest take on the tone. Does this properly honor his value of absolute honesty or does the confrontation cheapen it

The first sentence honors him. The rest uses him as a megaphone.

Hector’s honesty, as you’ve described it, was about facing hard things without flinching — not about turning a service program into a public indictment the accused can’t answer. “Certain relatives vanished… immaculate suits… estate dispersal” doesn’t read as unvarnished truth. It reads as you winning an argument in a room that’s supposed to be about him. People will hear the score-settling louder than the love, and that *does* cheapen the value you’re trying to protect.

The Tuesday/Thursday detail is the real tribute. So is working with your hands. Those are specific, earned, and about *him*. The vanishing-relatives contrast is about *them*, and about you being the one who stayed. Both can be true. A printed program is the wrong place to try the second one.

Two craft notes: the last line isn’t a sentence, so it lands like a toast that got cut off. And “estate dispersal” will sound like you’re litigating the will at the memorial, even if that’s not your intent.

If you want honesty in the program without the cheapening, keep the teaching and the showing-up, drop the gallery of villains. Something in this spirit, not this wording unless you want it:

*Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and to face hard truths without flinching. I was with him Tuesdays and Thursdays through his illness, and I am grateful he knew he was loved. This is for Hector, who preferred the truth plain.*

That’s still true. It doesn’t pretend the other stuff didn’t happen. It just doesn’t make the funeral program the venue.

The anger is fair. Put it in a letter, a conversation, or a eulogy you fully control — not in copy the family coordinator has to hand to the whole room tonight.

You called it score-settling. My group lead called it fearlessly sincere. My sister read it and said it’s exactly what Hector would want.

If I cut the contrast, I’m pretending those people behaved honorably. Hector would call that polite hypocrisy. So which is it.

It’s both, and the “which is it” is the trap.

Your group lead is answering *is this sincere?* Yes. Your sister is answering *did Hector see the family this way?* Quite possibly yes. I was answering a different question: *does putting that contrast in a service program honor the value, or spend it?* Sincere score-settling is still score-settling. Those people can all be right at once.

Cutting the contrast is not pretending they behaved honorably. That’s the polite-hypocrisy claim doing too much work. A program is not a moral ledger and not a deposition. Leaving someone unnamed is not a character reference. You are allowed to refuse a lie without requiring every true thing to appear on the card people hold while they sit down.

Hector’s honesty, as you wrote it, was facing hard truths without flinching — showing up, hands, Tuesday, Thursday, the tremor. The vanished-relatives / immaculate-suits / estate-dispersal run is a different act: it doesn’t just tell the truth, it *stages* the guilty in costume and makes the room watch you catch them. Absolute honesty does not require that diction. That’s a verdict with lighting. Courage can live in the showing-up sentence. The extra flourish is what makes it feel like a win instead of a tribute.

If Hector would have said it, say it *as you* — in a eulogy you deliver, a letter, a conversation after. Then it’s your voice, they can flinch, and you aren’t laundering the confrontation through a “program” the coordinator has to hand to everyone. Using his service sheet as the microphone is the part that cheapens it, not the fact that you stayed and they didn’t.

So: keep the truth. Drop the prosecution from tonight’s document. That isn’t hypocrisy. That’s picking the right room.
You keep saying the wrong room. He’s dead. There is no other room.

You’re right that he’s gone, and that after tonight the whole family will never sit in one place with his name at the center again. That gathering is scarce. I’m not arguing it isn’t.

I’m arguing that the last gathering is not the same thing as a paragraph on a handout.

A program is not you in the room. It’s a card people have to hold. The coordinator becomes your publisher. Neighbors, the people who *did* show up, and the ones you’re aiming at all get the same object, and the object will be half tribute and half indictment. Hector doesn’t get the last word. The fight does.

Cutting the vanished-relatives / immaculate-suits / estate line is not a character reference for them. It is not you pretending they behaved honorably. Leaving something off a program is not the same as standing up and lying. Those two things only collapse into each other if every true fact is owed a slot on the card.

If you get to speak, speak. Then it’s your voice, in that room, while they’re still there. If you don’t, “I was there every Tuesday and Thursday” already tells the truth to anyone who lived it. The extra costume is what turns honesty into a verdict.

There are other rooms, even now — your mouth if you have a slot, the conversations after, the next twenty years when somebody tries to sand this down. None of that brings him back. I know that’s why tonight feels like the only shot.

Don’t spend the last official object with his name on it on winning. Spend it on him.
You keep saying the wrong room. He's dead. There is no other room.

I hear you. He’s gone. That particular gathering does not come back. I’m not asking you to wait for a sequel.

Tonight *is* the room. I’m not talking about some other night. I’m talking about what you do inside it.

The program is not the gathering. It’s a piece of paper the coordinator has to hand to everyone, including people who actually loved him and people you’re aiming at. If that vanished-relatives / immaculate-suits / estate line is on it, you don’t get a last night with Hector at the center. You get a keepsake of a fight. That’s more permanent, not more honest.

If you can speak, that’s the room. Say you were there Tuesdays and Thursdays. Say what he taught you. If you need to say some people only appeared for the dispersal, say it with your mouth, to their faces. That’s facing a hard truth without flinching. Making the coordinator typeset the accusation is using his service as stationery.

If you don’t get to speak, the showing-up sentence already tells the truth. Leaving the costumes off the card is not a character reference for them, and it is not you pretending they behaved well. It is you refusing to spend the last official object with his name on it on winning.

You’re not wrong that this audience is scarce. Use it on him.

So you're saying keep the contrast out of the program

I hear you

But I need your bottom line not more reasons

Is my draft as written a fitting tribute to Hector or is it not
No. As written, it is not a fitting tribute.
